extracted.intended_audience: general public and prospective clients interested in personal-injury/product-liability facts
extracted.subtask_description: A law-firm blog summary correcting common misconceptions about the Stella Liebeck v. McDonald's coffee case, recounting factual findings from discovery, trial awards, expert testimony, and post-case developments. Useful for readers wanting a fuller factual account rather than popularized summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case caption and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella Liebeck v. McDonald's Restaurants, P.T.S., Inc. and McDonald's International, Inc. — a New Mexico case decided in 1994.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the precise case caption and jurisdiction when summarizing or citing the matter; facts and rulings come from that New Mexico litigation record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate factual context (who was driver,vehicle state)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella Liebeck was a 79 year-old passenger in her grandson’s car; the vehicle was stopped when she spilled the coffee (contrary to initial insurance-company reports that misidentified her as driver or said the car was moving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting the case, correct common misstatements (e.g., passenger vs driver; car stopped vs moving). Misreporting alters perceived negligence and culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of injuries and medical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella suffered full-thickness burns (third-degree) over 6% of her body (inner thighs, perineum, buttocks, genital/groin areas) and lesser burns over 16% of her body; hospitalized eight days, underwent skin grafting and debridement, lost almost 20% body weight, treated for two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific medical facts (burn degree, % body surface, hospitalization, surgeries, long-term treatment) to justify compensatory damages and counter minimalist characterizations of the injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior incidents / notice to defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Between 1982 and 1992, McDonald's had more than 700 claims as a result of people burning themselves on their coffee; some involved third-degree burns similar to Stella’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting a significant number of prior claims supports arguments of corporate notice and reckless conduct; include nature and severity of prior incidents where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate coffee-temperature policy
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's actively enforced a requirement that all franchisees hold the coffee in the pot at between 185 and 190 degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report internal corporate standards and policies precisely — such policies can be central evidence of unreasonably dangerous practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry standard temperature comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all other fast-food franchises hold their coffee at 135 to 140 degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare defendant practices to industry norms to show deviation from accepted safety standards; stating other franchises' typical temperatures provides context for dangerousness claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness for human consumption assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's agreed that 180 degree coffee is not 'fit for human consumption' because it would immediately scald; they assumed people would wait before attempting to drink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting defendant admissions about product unfitness is powerful; note any internal reasoning (e.g., assumption consumers will wait) and its legal relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermodynamics / expert testimony on burn risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermodynamics experts testified that coffee at 180 degrees will cause third-degree burns in two to seven seconds, whereas at 150 degrees Stella would likely have received no burns at all (maybe slight reddening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include expert measurements and causal timelines (temperature → burn severity → time to injury) when assessing product danger and causation; expert evidence can quantify risk differences between temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer knowledge / expectation of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's argued most customers preferred their coffee hot but admitted on cross-examination most customers probably didn’t know their coffee was hot enough to cause full-thickness, third-degree burns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between asserted customer preferences and actual customer knowledge; lack of informed expectation supports claims of unreasonable danger or inadequate warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-lawsuit settlement negotiation and offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Stella attempted to negotiate directly with McDonald's and asked for $20,000.00 (roughly her 'out-of-pocket' expenses); McDonald's offered $800.00.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting pre-suit settlement offers and demands can show defendant's unwillingness to fairly compensate and may be used to infer reasonableness of litigation and need for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensatory damages awarded and basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury awarded $200,000.00 in compensatory damages for past and future medical bills, lost wages, disfigurement, and pain and suffering, reduced by 20% for comparative negligence to $160,000.00.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining awards, list the compensatory categories and note reductions for comparative negligence to show how damages were calculated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative negligence applied
rubrics_metrics.description: The compensatory damage award was reduced by 20% for Stella’s own comparative negligence for opening the lid while it was in her lap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for any plaintiff fault and how it proportionally reduces awards; specify the conduct deemed negligent and the percentage reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punitive damages rationale and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury awarded $2.7 million in punitive damages after hearing testimony about the coffee being 40 to 50 degrees hotter than industry standard, many severe injuries beforehand, and McDonald's ignoring prior attempts to get them to turn the temperature down. The jury arrived at $2.7 million as it represents about two days of McDonald’s coffee sales; the judge later reduced punitive damages to $480,000.00.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain punitive damages as punishment/deterrence tied to reprehensibility and, in this case, relative corporate revenue; report both jury award and any judicial reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-trial measurements / remedial changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent investigation found that the temperature of coffee at the local Albuquerque McDonald’s was between 155 and 160 degrees Fahrenheit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note post-litigation measurements or changes (policy or practice adjustments) as evidence of remedial action or to show variability across locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and appellate posture
rubrics_metrics.description: McDonald's appealed the verdict, and the parties agreed to settle the case for a confidential sum before the Appellate Court ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing outcomes, include whether appeals proceeded or the case settled and whether settlement terms are confidential; this affects whether the appellate precedent is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countering simplified public narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The insurance company’s press releases oversimplified and misrepresented the case (e.g., 'old lady spilled coffee and recovered millions'); the article aims to 'give you the rest of the story you won’t get' from those press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize correcting common myths by providing detailed factual context and discovery evidence; media soundbites often omit key facts relevant to legal assessment.
